title: How Do You Test a Feature That Isn't Deterministic? Testing LLM-Backed Features
excerpt: When the output changes every run, your test suite needs a fundamentally different mental model. Here's how I've been approaching LLM feature testing in production pipelines.
content:
When we shipped our first LLM-backed feature — a document summarization tool built on top of GPT-4o — our QA process fell apart within the first week. Not because the feature was broken, but because our entire test infrastructure was built on the assumption that the same input produces the same output. It doesn't, with LLMs. Call the same prompt twice and you'll get two perfectly valid but completely different summaries. Our CI pipeline started lighting up red for all the wrong reasons, and we had a real conversation about whether traditional test automation even applied here.

It does. But you have to rebuild your mental model almost from scratch.

The challenge isn't that LLMs are untestable — it's that the properties you can assert on are fundamentally different. You're no longer verifying exact outputs. You're verifying *qualities* of outputs. That shift sounds simple, but it changes your entire tooling stack, your CI integration strategy, and what you treat as a passing test.

## Stop Asserting on Content, Start Asserting on Properties

![](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1629654297299-c8506221ca97?w=800&q=80)


The first mistake I made was writing tests that looked like this:

```python
def test_summary():
    result = summarize(document)
    assert result == "The report covers Q3 revenue growth of 12%..."
```

That's a dead end. The correct assertion for a summarization feature isn't about what the output says — it's about what it does and doesn't do. Does it stay within a certain length? Does it contain no claims not present in the source document? Does it mention the document's key entities?

These are property-based checks. In practice, they break down into four categories that I've found reliable across different LLM features:

**Structural properties** — Does the output match the expected format? If you're returning JSON, does it parse? If you're returning a bulleted list, does it have the right number of items? These are pure code assertions and they're the most stable part of your suite.

**Boundary conditions** — What happens when you send an empty string, a 50,000-token document, or a prompt in a language the model wasn't tuned for? These are the edge cases where LLMs still fail loudly and consistently enough to catch with hard assertions.

**Semantic properties** — Does the output correctly reflect the input? This is where it gets hard, because you need another model to evaluate it. More on that below.

**Behavioral invariants** — Properties that must hold regardless of output content. "The response must never include the user's raw system prompt." "The response must not claim to be a human." These can be encoded as regex checks, classifier calls, or secondary LLM evaluations.

The structural and behavioral invariant tests should go in your standard pytest suite and run on every commit. They're fast, cheap, and reliable. The semantic tests need their own lane.

## The Eval Suite: A Separate Pipeline for Semantic Quality

Semantic evaluation is the part of LLM testing that doesn't fit cleanly into unit testing. You can't assert that a summary is "faithful to the source document" with a string comparison. You need either a human or a model to make that judgment.

The pattern I've settled on is a dedicated eval suite, separated from the main test pipeline. It runs on PR merges and nightly — not on every commit, because it's expensive and slow.

The tooling I reach for here is [DeepEval](https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval), which gives you pytest-style test definitions around LLM-specific metrics. A faithfulness check for a RAG-backed feature looks like this:

```python
import pytest
from deepeval import assert_test
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase
from deepeval.metrics import FaithfulnessMetric, HallucinationMetric

@pytest.mark.llm_eval
def test_rag_faithfulness():
    context = [
        "Acme Corp reported Q3 2024 revenue of $4.2 billion, up 12% YoY.",
        "Operating margin was 18.5%.",
    ]
    test_case = LLMTestCase(
        input="What was Acme Corp's Q3 revenue growth?",
        actual_output=rag_pipeline.run("What was Acme Corp's Q3 revenue growth?"),
        retrieval_context=context,
    )
    assert_test(test_case, [FaithfulnessMetric(threshold=0.8), HallucinationMetric(threshold=0.2)])
```

DeepEval uses an LLM-as-a-judge under the hood — it sends your output and context to an evaluation model (typically GPT-4 or a local model) and gets back a score. The threshold approach means you're not asserting on a single right answer, you're asserting on a quality floor. That's the mental shift that makes semantic eval work.

Beyond DeepEval, Braintrust is worth knowing about if your team is more platform-oriented. It handles the experiment tracking layer better — you can compare eval runs across prompt versions and model versions in a dashboard rather than reading CI logs. For teams where a PM or ML engineer is also reviewing eval results, that matters.

## LLM-as-Judge: Making It Reliable Enough for CI

![](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1587620962725-abab7fe55159?w=800&q=80)


Using a language model to evaluate another language model's output sounds circular, but it works — with caveats. The biggest practical problem is that the judge model is also non-deterministic, which means your eval scores can drift between runs even when nothing changed.

The fix is straightforward: set temperature to 0 on your judge model. This doesn't make the judge perfectly deterministic across all inputs, but it eliminates the run-to-run variance that makes trend tracking noisy. Every LLM eval framework I've used, including DeepEval and Latitude, recommends this.

The second problem is bias. Judge models tend to prefer longer, more confident-sounding answers, and they can be gamed by outputs that are stylistically polished but semantically wrong. The mitigation I use is running the same judgment call multiple times with slightly different system prompts and taking the majority vote — a technique sometimes called self-consistency. Patronus AI documents this as running the same input through the judge three times; if results are inconsistent, you revise the evaluation prompt rather than trust the score.

I've also learned to treat LLM-as-a-judge as a regression detector, not an absolute quality meter. If your faithfulness score drops from 0.87 to 0.71 after a prompt change, that's signal worth investigating — even if you can't say with certainty that 0.87 is "good." The delta matters more than the number.

## Fitting Evals into Your CI/CD Pipeline

This is where most teams get it wrong, and where I've made the most mistakes. You can't gate every PR on a full eval run — it's too slow (5–15 minutes per run depending on dataset size) and too expensive ($0.02–$0.10 per test case with GPT-4 as judge). But you also can't skip eval entirely and trust your unit tests to catch semantic regressions.

The structure that's worked for me across two different products:

**Fast gate (runs on every PR, < 2 minutes):**
- Structural tests: JSON schema validation, length checks, format assertions
- Behavioral invariants: prompt injection resistance, PII leakage checks, response boundary assertions
- A small smoke eval suite of 10–15 golden cases with hard thresholds

**Slow gate (runs on merge to main and nightly):**
- Full eval suite against a versioned golden dataset of 100–200 cases
- Comparison against baseline scores from the previous week
- Results posted to a Slack channel with a pass/fail + delta summary

The golden dataset is the part that requires the most maintenance. You need to keep it version-controlled alongside your prompts. When you update a prompt, you may need to update expected quality thresholds. When you switch model versions — say from gpt-4o to gpt-4o-mini for cost reasons — you need to re-run the baseline and decide what quality degradation is acceptable.

For the nightly gate in GitHub Actions, the workflow looks like:

```yaml
name: LLM Eval Suite
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  eval:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install deepeval pytest
      - name: Run eval suite
        env:
          OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
        run: pytest tests/evals/ -m llm_eval --tb=short
```

One thing I'd add: version-pin your evaluation model. If you're using GPT-4o as your judge, pin to a specific snapshot (e.g., `gpt-4o-2024-08-06`) rather than the `gpt-4o` alias. OpenAI updates the alias without notice, and a model update can shift your scores without any change to your product — which means false regressions and a broken pipeline trust.

## What Good Test Coverage Looks Like for an LLM Feature

After going through this on a few different features — summarization, a customer support chatbot, a code explanation tool — here's the distribution I've landed on:

- 60% structural + behavioral invariant tests (standard pytest, fast, cheap)
- 25% semantic eval on a golden dataset (DeepEval or similar, slow gate)
- 10% shadow testing in production (real traffic, score logged but not gated)
- 5% manual red-teaming sessions on new model versions or major prompt changes

Shadow testing is underused in QA conversations about LLMs and it's one of the most valuable signals I have. Running your eval metrics against real production traffic and logging the scores — without gating on them — tells you whether your golden dataset is actually representative of what users are sending. Twice I've caught prompt regressions through shadow scoring that my golden dataset completely missed, because users were phrasing questions in ways I hadn't anticipated.

The thing I want to leave you with: LLM testing is not a solved problem, and anyone who tells you their eval suite gives them full confidence is either running a very narrow feature or overstating their coverage. What you're building is a system that catches regressions reliably and characterizes quality over time. That's different from a test suite that tells you whether the software is correct — and getting comfortable with that distinction is the real shift that makes LLM testing tractable.
